title: Many to Many Relationships & Aliases
summary: Explains many to many relationships as two one-to-many links joined through a third (junction) table, builds student/class/enrollment, joins all three tables, and introduces aliases with AS for columns and tables.

concepts.heading: What many to many means
points: A student takes many classes, and a class has many students. Two one-to-many relationships facing each other give many to many.
It is rarer and more complex than the other types.
A single foreign key cannot model it, so Postgres designs use a third table (a junction or link table) holding one row per pairing.

concepts.heading: The enrollment junction table
points: Each enrollment row has a student_id and a class_id, e.g. student 1 in class 1, student 1 in class 3, student 2 in class 1.
In a design diagram this appears as student (one) to enrollment (many) and class (one) to enrollment (many), rather than one direct many-to-many line.
enrollment declares student_id INTEGER REFERENCES student(id) and class_id INTEGER REFERENCES class(id): both are foreign keys.
PRIMARY KEY (student_id, class_id) is a composite key: the pair is unique, so the same student cannot be enrolled in the same class twice. No separate id column is needed.
class table: id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(45) (a string capped at 45 characters).

concepts.heading: Sample data
points: Add a second student (Jack Bauer, id 2) and three classes: English Literature (1), Maths (2), Physics (3), ids assigned in insertion order by SERIAL.
Enroll student 1 in classes 1 and 2, and student 2 in classes 2 and 3. Two separate INSERTs are used for readability but one could hold all four tuples.

concepts.heading: Joining three tables
points: Start FROM enrollment, then chain two JOINs: student ON student.id = enrollment.student_id, and class ON class.id = enrollment.class_id.
Result has one row per enrollment record, with student and class details repeated as needed.
Such a table can answer questions: how many students take maths (2), which classes one student takes, which classes two students share.

concepts.heading: Aliases
points: AS renames an output column: student.id AS stud makes that column header stud. Useful when several tables each have an id column.
Tables can also be aliased: FROM enrollment AS e JOIN student AS s ..., then use s.id and e.student_id in place of the full names. This shortens long queries.
The AS keyword is optional for tables: FROM enrollment e works the same.
Recommendation given: keep AS for column aliases in SELECT for readability, even though it is optional.
(Extra) Once a table is aliased, the original name can no longer be used for it in that query.

task.name: Create the many-to-many tables and query them
task.starting_point: school database with student, contact_detail and homework_submission tables.
task.goal: Add class and enrollment, insert data, run the double join and experiment with aliases.
steps: Create the class and enrollment tables.
Insert Jack Bauer as a student, the three classes and the four enrollment rows.
Run the three-table join with SELECT *.
Change the select to use AS stud for the student id.
Rewrite the query with table aliases e, s and c, with and without AS.
task.expected_result: Four rows, each pairing a student with a class; the aliased versions return identical data with a renamed id column.

solution_code.code:
SELECT s.id AS id, first_name, last_name, title
FROM enrollment e
JOIN student s ON s.id = e.student_id
JOIN class c ON c.id = e.class_id;

task.reference_repo_path: Section 33 - PostgreSQL/33.13 - Many to Many Relationships & Aliases/queries.sql

pitfalls: Inserting an enrollment pair twice violates the composite primary key.
Referencing a student or class id that does not exist fails the foreign key.
Using the full table name after aliasing it.
Ambiguous id column when selecting without a prefix.
